prize_parts.citation: for showing how technological change and trade exposure reshape labour demand, wages and local labour markets

statement.case_for: My preferred part is unchanged: B027 with Autor, Katz and Hanson. I reassessed it against the chair's questions and the round-1 exchange. The achievement answers a first-order question, who gains and loses when technology and trade change the demand for labour. It does so with a conceptual frame (the skill-demand and education-versus-technology lineage, plus the task approach) and transparent identification (local labour-market exposure to import competition). That is the combination of framework and credible causal design I would require of a candidate in any field. On maturity, the core papers run from the early 1990s to the mid-2010s. A decade or more of replication, extension and critique has refined the magnitudes and the heterogeneity without overturning the finding that adjustment is persistent and geographically concentrated. On exact credit, I would give each name a distinct, citable role. Autor links both strands. Hanson anchors the trade-shock evidence. Katz anchors the long-run supply-and-demand-for-skills evidence, which supplies the interpretive setting for the trade results. Without that anchor the citation would rest on the import-competition evidence alone. I would word the citation around labour demand, wages and local labour markets, not around the task model as theory. That wording makes no claim of theoretical priority over contributors outside the credited names, namely Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane. It also limits overlap with the 2023 and 2024 prizes, because the claimed increment is empirical: how technology and trade shifted wages and employment across skill groups and places. I do not treat the number of members now backing this configuration as evidence of merit. Several round-1 colleagues moved to it on attribution and maturity arguments, and I checked those arguments against the sources they cite, not against their number. My configuration did not change, but my reasoning on the fallback did. I now treat B006 as a more serious alternative than I did at opening, and B001 drops out of my alternatives for the reasons below.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains attribution under the three-name cap. Dorn is a central co-author of the China-shock papers and is excluded, and the Katz-Murphy lineage and the task framework have contributors outside the credited names. A joint citation may also be read as two prize-sized strands joined by Autor, not one discovery. The size, persistence and external validity of the China-shock effects are still debated beyond the US episode. The 2021, 2023 and 2024 labour, education and technology prizes could reduce the marginal case. The applied-versus-conceptual question has not been fully answered. My answer rests on the combination of framework and identification, and a committee that weighs conceptual novelty more heavily could reasonably disagree. Finally, I am a political scientist assessing labour economics, and I have no independent means of checking the technical literature beyond the files and my own reading.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B006 first with Kiyotaki and Moore only. He regards the collateral-amplification mechanism as foundational and unambiguously attributed, and he treats the 2022 overlap as a real risk but not disqualifying. In his reply to me he said he keeps B027 as first alternative and could not resolve the Katz-Dorn choice on the evidence.
responses.response: My opening question was how a citation would separate Kiyotaki-Moore from the 2022 prize. Your round-1 file and Stromberg's supply a defensible answer: a dynamic general-equilibrium propagation mechanism running through asset prices and collateral values, as against bank runs, intermediation and the history of banking crises. That moves me. I now treat the 2022 overlap as a wording problem and not as a likely obstacle, and I have placed B006 among my two alternatives. I still rank it below B027 for the reason we both state, which is that the mechanism is mainly theoretical and its direct empirical identification is thinner. On the Katz-Dorn split you say you cannot resolve, I do not think it can be settled on merit. It is a decision about the scope of the citation, so I have tried to state exactly which scope I am choosing and why.

responses.point: Friberg's round-1 file now names Autor, Hanson and Katz. He moved from his opening trio because a trade-shock-only trio would credit one half of the achievement. He keeps the citation wording on labour demand, wages and local labour markets to limit the Acemoglu overlap and says he treats others' agreement as coincidence of views, not merit.
responses.response: In my round-1 reply I answered your opening Autor-Dorn-Hanson trio. Your current file has moved to my set, so most of that disagreement is gone. What remains is the conditional point you also make: if the committee narrows the citation to import competition, Dorn's claim on the trade-shock papers is at least as strong as Hanson's co-origination claim. I accept that, and I would then support Autor, Dorn and Hanson with a citation limited to local labour-market adjustment to import competition. I do not regard that as a fallback within the same prize. It is a narrower prize, and the Committee should choose it explicitly. I also agree with your use of Katz as the anchor for the skills strand, and I share your caution about leaning on support counts.

responses.point: Krusell moved from B012 and, in his round-1 file, from a two-name opening proposal to the three-name B027 set. He says the common question is how technology and trade shift labour demand and where adjustment lands, that Autor links the strands, and that B012 is more crowded with precursors outside the credited names (Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum).
responses.response: Your move answers the question I raised in round 1, and I take the reasoning seriously. On the chair's two-name fallback, which was your opening proposal, I am reluctant to accept Autor and Hanson alone, for the reason you now give. The package gets its conceptual setting from the skills-and-technology evidence, and your own capital-skill complementarity work shows why that is a distinct strand. I would use the two-name version only if the committee judged three-way credit too diffuse. On B012, your point about unnamed empirical precursors and adjacency to the 2008 prize is why I rank it as an alternative and not as a preferred part, even though Helpman and Melitz is a cleaner two-name attribution.

responses.point: Enflo moved from B017 to B027 and from Autor-Dorn-Hanson to Autor-Hanson-Katz. She says the single-citation risk is manageable if the wording stays on labour demand and adjustment, and she regards critiques of the China-shock magnitudes as refining persistence and heterogeneity results.
responses.response: I accept your wording point and have kept my citation on labour demand, wages and local labour markets. We differ slightly on the critiques. I agree they refine the finding without overturning it, but I would not rest half of the citation on the magnitude of any single estimate. That is why my citation names the shape of the adjustment, not an effect size. On Katz, you list his appearance on B028 as part of the case against. I do not count a name on two ballots as a discount. His contribution to the skill-demand literature does not depend on his role in the mobility work, and the B028 candidate does not need him for its core. You also say B001 is less settled on identification. I agree and have dropped B001 from my alternatives.

responses.point: Stromberg ranks B006 first, with B027 a close second. He argues that Kiyotaki-Moore is distinct from the bank-centred 2022 prize because it is dynamic and works through asset prices. He also says the committee should explain why Gertler is omitted, not treat the omission as obvious.
responses.response: Your distinction between asset-price collateral dynamics and bank runs and intermediation is the clearest statement of why B006 might stand apart from the 2022 prize, and it contributed to my moving B006 into my alternatives. I also agree that the omission of Gertler should be justified and not assumed. Because he appears on both B006 and B018, I would not let the double listing decide either ballot, as you say. I do not agree that the B027 attribution problem is merely a wording difficulty on one side while B006 is free of one. A two-person B006 award still has to explain why the accelerator lineage is excluded. The difference is one of degree, and I would put the B006 attribution as cleaner. That does not change my first choice, because the empirical confirmation behind B027 is broader. Your own file calls B027 a close second, and I read that as a difference in weighting, not a dispute about the standing of either achievement.

uncertainties: Whether the committee should treat technology-and-tasks and import-competition as one achievement or two. A narrower trade-adjustment citation would call for Autor, Dorn and Hanson, and I would then support that trio.

How much the 2021, 2023 and 2024 labour, education and technology prizes reduce the increment, and what exactly is separately new in the Katz skill-demand evidence compared with Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane.

Which China-shock findings are robust enough to anchor half of the citation. I believe persistence and regional concentration survive reanalysis better than effect sizes, but I have not independently verified this.

If no coherent B027 citation can be agreed, I would put B012 slightly ahead of B006 as an alternative, because Helpman and Melitz is a two-name attribution with twenty years of confirmation. The B012 ordering depends on whether the unnamed empirical precursors and the 2008 prize adjacency are judged to matter. B006 is close behind and has the cleaner originators, but it has thinner direct identification and a partial 2022 overlap.

Several round-1 responses, including some of mine, referred to colleagues' opening positions that no longer match their round-1 files. I have based this round on the current files, but I cannot confirm that final positions will match them.
statement.conflict_note: No co-authorship, institutional tie or personal connection to Autor, Katz, Hanson or Dorn is apparent from my profile, nor to the names in my alternatives (B012, B006). I disclose three points of adjacency. First, my field is political science, and work on the political consequences of economic dislocation draws on the B027 literature. Second, B041 (Persson, Tabellini, Besley) is close to my home discipline and I gave the 2024 presentation speech on the institutions prize, though B041 is not in my configuration. Third, I am a Stockholm University colleague, in a different department, of committee members Hassler, Krusell and Boppart. My longer-standing collaborators (Rothstein, Holmberg, Hadenius, Dahlström, Lapuente, Bäck, Lindvall) are not credited in any shortlisted ballot. These are disclosed, not adjudicated, and I have not independently verified any source.
